messages.subject: RNA-Seq, R, and Training
parts:
This is prompted by Noam Ross' tweet "Was asked about doing RNAseq work in R, which I know nothing about. Is this taught at the BioInf Core trainings?"

There are two overlapping questions here:  1) How is R used in RNA-Seq? 2) Is any R included in UCD Bioinformatics Core Training?
To simplify this, the following presumes RNA-Seq with Illumina HiSeq reads.  Typical compressed file sizes are 5-10G (fastq.gz) and ~10G (bam - compressed alignments)

1. R and RNA-Seq
For typical workflow, see slide 3 here. Good Bioconductor resources are high-throughput-sequencing and RNA-Seq tutorial. (There are many, many RNA-Seq Bioconductor packages)
Read QC, trimming, and alignment (to reference fasta) are typically done with C programs but there are R packages that perform these functions as well.  (Often, when processing these large files, the R package takes more time and RAM than do most of the equivalent C programs.)
Converting alignments to raw counts per gene can be done in R or with perl/python scripts.  This is a much smaller table.
Statistical analysis of raw counts (normalization, modeling, differential expression, FDR testing, etc.) is typically done in R, but a very common non-R RNA-Seq stats software is cuffdiff.
Downstream processing (data visualization, GO Enrichment, Pathway Analysis, etc.) is also commonly done with R packages (edgeR, DESeq, cummeRbund, etc.)
(Note: some software, notably Trinity, wraps R packages in perl or python scripts)

2. RNA-Seq Training (UCD Biocore)
(Note: Documentation from past courses is at http://training.bioinformatics.ucdavis.edu/documentation/)
Our typical trainee is a biologist (grad student/postdoc/researcher/faculty), with little or no exposure to command-line or programming languages. For the last few years we've used the Galaxy GUI platform to concentrate on concepts and workflows rather than the steep command-line learning curve. Although Galaxy is simple for the user, running R in Galaxy is a pain to set up and maintain, requiring XML wrappers to be written to generate the R scripts. So, our 2013 Short Course didn't include any R.  This year, we're teaching two week-long courses -- one in Galaxy and one in command-line.  Although the topics will be the same, the command-line course might let us try R again.
A few years ago, we experimented with a 2-day Data Visualization in R Workshop, using R Studio, which did cover some RNA-Seq analysis.  It was last taught in 2012, when Vince Buffalo was in our group. I would like to include some of these topics in a more focused RNA-Seq workshop (in late 2014 or 2015).  One challenge we have to teaching R is that most of the bioinformatics core personnel are not statisticians and are also not proficient R programmers. (I mainly "get by" following the vignettes.)

It would be great to get input from you on the incorporation of R into our workshops.  And maybe we could explain some of the challenges and opportunities with RNA-Seq. We could set up a meeting to discuss or come to one of the D-RUG meetings.

Thanks!

Monica Britton
